items.title: Madrid chief Pérez: "outrageous" that LaLiga president Tebas hasn't resigned
items.summary: Florentino Pérez hit out at Javier Tebas -- saying it was "outrageous" that the LaLiga president had not resigned his post -- and slammed Spanish football's handling of the Negreira case in a speech to Real Madrid members on Saturday, while also signalling a closer working relationship with former a
items.text:
Florentino Pérez hit out at Javier Tebas -- saying it was "outrageous" that the LaLiga president had not resigned his post -- and slammed Spanish football's handling of the Negreira case in a speech to Real Madrid members on Saturday, while also signalling a closer working relationship with former adversaries UEFA.
Pérez, who was re-elected as Madrid president earlier this year, delivered a 45-minute speech at the club's annual assembly, which began with applause for former tennis star Rafael Nadal, as he joined Madrid's board of directors.
In recent years, Pérez has used the assembly to deliver updates on a series of conflicts involving Madrid and football's governing bodies, including the attempted breakaway European Superleague, as well as the failure to bring the Negreira investigation -- into Barcelona's decades-long payments to Spain's former vice-president of refereeing -- to a conclusion.
"The Negreira case isn't just a problem for Real Madrid," Pérez said. "What happened was extraordinarily serious... It's not for me to judge anyone. The courts and UEFA will do that. But as Real Madrid president, I won't stop until those responsible are held accountable.
"It seems like the whole system wants us to forget about what happened, and talk about something else. The head of referees said we should move on. How are we going to move on? The worst is Tebas, who instead of helping to clarify it all, has chosen to attack Real Madrid every day... It's outrageous that he hasn't resigned."
Last month, Madrid called for Tebas to quit after he compared the club's communications policy to Nazi minister Joseph Goebbels, saying Madrid's use of its club TV channel "recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels."
Tebas responded to Pérez's speech in a series of posts on X on Saturday.
"Florentino, before you ask for my resignation again, read my Oct. 16 post in full," he said. "There I explained which Real Madrid TV communication techniques I was criticizing, and why. I stand by what I wrote. I have committed no wrongdoing."
Pérez also discussed Madrid's changing relationship with UEFA and European Football Clubs (formerly the European Club Association) in the wake of the Superleague row, following an agreement reached between the three parties in February.
"We've had important differences, but we've always put football's interests first," Pérez said, before appearing to break news of a joint initiative which would meet one of the Superleague's stated goals: broadcasting games free-to-air.
"From next season, the best European games will be shown for free in India on a new platform. It's a way of testing this model, in one of the biggest countries in the world... It's the same process that FIFA followed with the Club World Cup. I also announce that Real Madrid are working to return to the EFC, and to UEFA's committees. We'll push for all these initiatives from the inside."
"Now it turns out that Florentino is the spokesperson for UEFA, the EFC and [their joint venture] UC3," Tebas responded. "He announces their TV plans before they do themselves."
- Tennis great Rafa Nadal accepts Real Madrid offer to join board of directors
- Veteran GK Courtois extends Real Madrid contract to 2028
- José Mourinho wants Vinícius Jr. to move on from summer woes
Pérez failed to elaborate on a plan which was much debated during Madrid's presidential elections earlier this year, to change the club's ownership structure by selling a percentage to an external investor.
Madrid are one of just four Spanish football clubs which are owned by their members. "I want to say again that Real Madrid won't be sold, it will never be sold," Pérez said on Saturday. "It belongs to its members... A year ago, I told you that we had to protect ourselves from threats both outside and inside. This year we've seen that, during the electoral campaign.
"I want you to leave here with a clear idea. Real Madrid is ours, not just in a romantic way, but truly. We need the members, more than ever, to be the active guardians of our financial wealth. That's why we're working on this reform, to protect the heritage that we've built. We won't adopt any decision that risks the ownership of the club by its members."
Later, facing questions from club members, Pérez called on fans not to whistle the players at the Bernabéu when the team underperforms.
"I just want to say one thing: you can't whistle our players," Pérez said. "The enemy is on the outside, not at home... I'd ask you never to support those whistles, which are influenced by some of the media."
The club's CEO, José Ángel Sánchez, also claimed there was now "no legal impediment" to holding concerts at the Bernabéu, after they were halted following noise concerns from neighbours.
"The acoustic work has finished, and it's improved a lot," Sánchez said. "We're thinking about bringing the concerts back soon."

items.text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

items.text:
Chaudhary helps Australia beat England in T20 shake-off of scandal-hit run
Australia beat England by three wickets with only one ball to spare as Nikhil Chaudhary’s 66 leads the charge in Melbourne.
Nikhil Chaudhary blasted 66 and a late cameo from Jack Edwards helped Australia edge past England by three wickets with a ball to spare in the opening T20 International of the series.
Chaudhary’s 38-ball knock was crucial, but it was Edwards’ late flurry that got the job done, with the fast-bowler hitting an unbeaten 25 off 11 as they chased down a victory target of 188 on Saturday.
It ensured they took a 1-0 lead in the five-match series and temporarily lifted some of the clouds hanging over Australian cricket. Four of the country’s previous five matches have resulted in defeats, including a 2-1 One-Day International home series defeat by England.
The win also came on the day that Cricket Australia backed Pat Cummins to stay on as Test captain, despite continued allegations that he and the rest of the 2018 team were aware of the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball during their tour of South Africa.
England captain Harry Brook’s quickfire 65 had guided the visitors to 187-9 – the highest T20I score at the Melbourne Cricket Ground – but Australia’s response had already begun prior to the chase when their bowlers restricted the end of the tourists’ innings that had looked set to comfortably pass 200.
“Right, there is the future of the Australian cricket side with those young guys in it,” said Australia captain Mitchell Marsh.
“They’re a great bunch. Hopefully a win like that gives them a lot of confidence that they all belong.”
The run chase started badly for Australia with opener Jake Fraser-McGurk falling to just his third ball, undone by the spin of Liam Dawson.
Australia got going when debutant Sam Harper came in and took 20 off Jamie Overton’s first over.
But the 29-year-old swung the bat once too often and departed for 32 off 15 balls, earning new England fast-bowler Henry Crocombe a first T20 wicket.
They were 86-2 at the halfway mark, and when Dawson took a stunning catch to remove Marsh for 37, Australia’s hopes appeared to rest with Tim David.
But the big-hitter struggled to get going and was out for 20, leaving Chaudhary, in only his fourth T20 for Australia, in charge.
He departed chasing another boundary, only for Edwards to step up.
They needed 11 of the last over from Sam Curran, and when Edwards smacked a six off the first delivery, they were on their way to the win.
“Very entertaining to go down to the last couple of balls,” said Brook. “We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface.”
Earlier, England lost opener Phil Salt to the first ball and they were 13-2 in the third over after Aneurin Donald was also removed cheaply for 10.
But Brook went to town, smacking three straight sixes from paceman Riley Meredith.
He reached 50 off 20 deliveries before his fiery knock ended when he got a faint outside edge off Chaudhary to wicketkeeper Harper.
Tom Banton was put down on 11, among six dropped catches by Australia, but his luck ran out on 39 when another debutant, Lachlan Shaw, held on to a difficult chance.
The wickets kept tumbling with Curran caught out on 21 and Will Jacks out lbw for three, with Jordan Cox hitting 27 to keep the scoreboard moving.

Uncapped Durham opener Ben McKinney replaces Jacob Bethell in England Test squad for South Africa after he was ruled out with a knee injury; England's white-ball side sweating on the fitness of Will Jacks
items.text:
Ben McKinney earns England Test call up for South Africa series as Jacob Bethell's replacement
Uncapped Durham opener Ben McKinney replaces Jacob Bethell in England Test squad for South Africa after he was ruled out with a knee injury; England's white-ball side sweating on the fitness of Will Jacks after suffering a finger injury in their series-opening T20I defeat to Australia
Saturday 21 November 2026 13:58, UK
England have added Ben McKinney to their Test squad touring South Africa next month, with the uncapped Durham opener serving as a replacement for the injured Jacob Bethell.
McKinney, a 6ft 7in left-handed batter, has become a regular in the England Lions set-up and underlined his growing reputation on this month's tour of St Kitts, hitting 145 against West Indies A.
He will provide competition and cover for England's top order that includes county colleague Emilio Gay.
Bethell underwent a second bout of knee surgery on Thursday after being ruled out of the series due to an ongoing issue that also required an operation in the summer.
The 23-year-old had linked up with England's white-ball squad in Australia earlier this month, only for his anticipated comeback to be cut short by a flare-up of his knee injury.
England's the three-Test series in South Africa gets under way in Johannesburg on December 17.
Jacks an injury doubt for rest of white-ball series in Australia
Meanwhile, England's white-ball side could be scrambling to find a captain by the end of their Australia tour after Will Jacks suffered a bloody finger injury in the closing moments of their series-opening T20I loss in Melbourne on Saturday.
Jacks hade to leave the field in the penultimate over of the three-wicket defeat with blood streaming from his right hand following a painful attempted caught-and-bowled off Ben Dwarshuis.
Jacks had been set to captain England for the first time in the fifth and final T20 in Canberra, with regular white-ball skipper Harry Brook having brought forward his departure ahead of next month's Test tour of South Africa.
"I don't know [how bad it is],-he obviously came off with a lot of blood but I couldn't quite see what happened," Brook said of Jacks' funger after Saturday's loss at the MCG.
"Hopefully he is alright because he has been such a valuable player for us in the last two years. It would be sad to see him go home early.
"I've not even thought about that one [the captaincy] yet, that's a decision we'll have to discuss but I don't have an answer yet."

items.title: Perspective: Defining 'human'
items.summary:
Perspective: Defining 'human'
The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrationa
items.text:
Perspective: Defining 'human'
The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrational fear of having no mobile phone service–although, given all the recent cyber-struggles, why would that be irrational?
The Cambridge 2026 World of the Year is … human. As in us. And perhaps humanity could stand some recognition in times when people see Artificial Intelligence seep into our lives the way ancient dinosaurs may have watched the asteroid plunge through the atmosphere, and think, "They're coming for us!" though I suspect a few T-Rexes might have said, "Hey, don't worry! We're too big to fail!"
Cambridge defines "human" as: "(h)aving the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines," but they don't specify much about what those qualities, faults and feelings are.
I'd say that humans have a sense of responsibility. We can say, "I'm sorry, that's my fault," when we screw up or fall short, as opposed to screens that just flash, SYSTEM OVERLOAD or UPDATE IN PROGRESS, 12% COMPLETE.
Humans seek joy, not just continued existence. Laughter, tears, love, spice, poetry, and all that jazz, not just code or text. Humans like jokes and prayers. We're driven by feelings, not just steered by algorithms. Love, fear, anger, desire, joy, and courage, excited by events, nerves and hormones – combine to make us unpredictable, irreverent and unreliable. But our experiences can also instill judgement; an appreciation for what's important; what endures; and what makes the lives we have worth living and savoring.
Making human the 2026 Word of the Year may remind us that we human beings, unlike any robots we have yet devised, have a sense of our own fragility. We know we don't last forever. And so it is important to strive, laugh, and love while we have the chance. The Cambridge dictionary leaves what human truly means to us.

items.summary:

- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in
items.text:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

items.text:
Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.
A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.
Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”
If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.
Here is what we know.
What is the Riemann hypothesis?
First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.
Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.
“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.
“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”
It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.
What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?
Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.
He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.
Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.
“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.
“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”
He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.
Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?
“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”
Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.
“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”
He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”
Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.
“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.
“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”
Why has it remained so elusive for so long?
“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.
“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”
He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.

Two drones have struck a cargo ship bound for Russia’s exclave Kaliningrad in international waters of the Gulf of Finland, clos
items.text:
Russia says Kaliningrad-bound ship struck by drones in Gulf of Finland
Two drones attack a cargo ship close to Russia’s maritime border, causing damage and crew evacuation.
Two drones have struck a cargo ship bound for Russia’s exclave Kaliningrad in international waters of the Gulf of Finland, close to Russia’s maritime border, according to a senior Russian official.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
It is not clear who was behind the attack.
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the vessel’s crew were being evacuated and the damage had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of St Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.
The ministry said air and sea traffic restrictions were a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.
“A Russian cargo ship is on fire in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Finnish Border Guard is leading the maritime rescue operation and is preparing for potential environmental damage control within Finland’s area of responsibility,” Finland’s Border Guard said on its official website.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns about striking in the area with Kyiv afterwards.
Saturday’s attack has not been attributed to anyone.

items.title: Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad
items.summary:
German government sees a global deterioration in religious freedom
November 21, 2026
The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas R
items.text:
German government sees a global deterioration in religious freedom
November 21, 2026
The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.
The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.
Authoritarian regimes increase pressure on religious communities
The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.
At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."
The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.
Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.
In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans, and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.
One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.
The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.
Intimidation reaches beyond borders
The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.
Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.
These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.
China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.
Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

items.text:
Sudan’s elderly face hardship and heartbreak in a life of displacement
Sudan’s displaced elderly often have to support grandchildren or fend for themselves.
Khartoum, Sudan – Hamad Mohammed Adam, 70, should be spending his days surrounded by his family and enjoying the comfort of life in his home village. Instead, he finds himself among hundreds of displaced elderly people in a camp in western Omdurman, with little between him and death.
Three months ago, Adam’s life changed when the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary attacked his village near Bara, northern Kordofan. He followed the rest of the village and fled, leaving behind his home, belongings and most painfully, his family.
“It was an early morning last August when the Rapid Support Forces militia invaded our village near Bara. It was a terrifying morning; they were killing everyone, women, men, children,” he said. “I ran with some friends and spent days to reach Omdurman. I am lucky that I have survived, but I am worried about my family.”
The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF paramilitary, two former military allies now engaged in a bitter power struggle for Sudan since April 2023, has affected all parts of the country. When fighting erupts in one area, residents are often forced to flee to another, where they lack jobs, a home, or a support base.
After travelling for about 300km (186 miles), Adam found himself in western Omdurman, close to the capital Khartoum. Today, he resides at al-Moulih camp for displaced people in western Omdurman, home to approximately 10,000 people, with those aged over 65 accounting for about one in five residents.
His escape from the fighting between the SAF and RSF, which has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, was only the start of his troubles. Adam knows nothing about the whereabouts of his family, and they don’t know where he is.
Lacking the support of his family, Adam’s immediate concern is finding enough food, medication and healthcare to survive. But the uncertainty of his family’s fate weighs heavily on him every day.
In the same camp, Aisha Alneel, 70, has lost more than her home: The security, independence and family connections that once shaped her life. She’s accompanied by her 72-year-old sister who needs medical attention, and her greatest hope is to reunite with her family and regain some sense of normality.
“I came to Port Sudan two years ago after losing my home in Khartoum. My plan is to travel with my older sister, but we faced financial strain,” she said. “We preferred to stay at this displacement camp in Port Sudan until we have enough money to leave.”
Sudan’s older population, classified as aged above 65 by the United Nations, is 1.8 million people in 2026, accounting for 3.5% of the population, according to the UN’s Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia.
Many elderly displaced people depend on regular medical supervision and assistance with everyday activities. When conflict forces them to abandon their homes, families, and familiar environments, these essential support systems can disappear overnight. It also disrupts or destroys the infrastructure and services they relied on to maintain a dignified life.
Traditionally, Sudanese families and local communities played a central role in caring for older relatives. Younger family members often assisted with food, medical appointments and daily needs, but the war has seen families scattered across Sudan and the country’s social fabric destroyed.
Living standards have plunged to levels last seen in the early 1990s, making it difficult for families to survive, let alone provide support to others. The UNDP has noted that Sudan’s economy has shrunk by more than 40 percent since the war broke out, and extreme poverty is expected to rise above 60 percent. This has placed additional pressure on institutions responsible for caring for older people.
At Al-Daw Hajooj home for the elderly, the management faces the difficult task of providing care to senior citizens amid a wider humanitarian crisis.
Moubarak Satti, director of Al-Daw Hajooj, told Al Jazeera that the home has 11 seniors and the situation remains “difficult” due to a lack of financial support needed to run the elderly care programmes.
“Like many institutions, we have been severely affected by the war. We lost our only vehicle, which we use it to transport elderly people to medical facilities; we lost many people during the conflict due to the lack of medical care,” Satti said.
“We welcome financial support from the community, NGOs, and international humanitarian organisations to continue providing care and essential services to older people.”
This requires more than emergency food assistance. It needs a coordinated response that recognises elderly people as a particular group with specific needs, said Satti.
The strain of displacement also impacts older people’s mental and emotional wellbeing. Separation from children and grandchildren, uncertainty about the future, and feelings of anxiety and helplessness can create intense feelings of isolation, government officials have said.
The Khartoum State Ministry of Social Development has provided support to vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, coordinating social protection services and working with relevant institutions to respond to the needs of displaced communities.
But the scale of the problem is staggering, with about 8.6 million people currently displaced. Attacks on civilian areas have also severely disrupted public services, making government and NGO support increasingly challenging, Minister of Social Welfare Siddig Ferini told Al Jazeera.
“We have reunited dozens of elderly displaced people with their families in many Sudanese states, while others are still searching for loved ones,” Ferini said. “We call on humanitarian organisations, donors, and philanthropists to support elderly people through social care and essential services, especially amid the ongoing war and

items.text:
Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

items.text:
Israeli attacks on Gaza kill at least four Palestinians
Three Palestinians were killed in an Israeli drone attack while a Palestinian man was killed by gunfire in Jabalia.
Israeli attacks in Gaza have killed at least four Palestinians in violation of last year’s “ceasefire”, as winter flooding deepens the humanitarian crisis in the enclave.
At least three people were killed when the car they were travelling in was struck by an Israeli drone on Saturday in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. Separately, a Palestinian man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Halawa displacement camp, east of northern Gaza’s Jabalia refugee camp.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire”, which came into force last October.
The ongoing attacks on the enclave coincide with a surge in pogroms carried out by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Late on Friday, Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was shot dead by security guards from an illegal Israeli settlement near the village of Dura al-Qar, north of Ramallah.
The Palestinian Health Ministry said his body was being withheld by Israeli authorities. Another Palestinian man was detained during the incident.
Reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers have been carrying out attacks with “impunity”.
“Less than 3 percent of Israeli attacks that are investigated lead to a partial or full conviction by Israeli authorities. Also, the number of settler attacks reported to Israeli authorities is very, very low because Palestinians are often detained, questioned or harassed for filing reports against violent settlers,” Odeh reported.
The violence inflicted on Palestinians in the West Bank has been condemned by Israeli allies, including the United Kingdom. Critics say Western leaders have not supported their rhetoric with sufficient action.
Earlier this month, an Al Jazeera investigation found that the UK had awarded $14.4m in new public contracts to firms with links to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, despite recently announcing a ban on importing goods from such settlements.
The British government has also sanctioned companies involved in settlement expansion.
Winter weather has compounded the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, with the World Food Programme (WFP) warning earlier this week that Palestinians have been forced to burn rubbish to cook their food.
“Now even the rubbish is wet,” warned Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director for Palestine.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said that more than 100,000 tents in Egypt cannot be delivered to Gaza due to strict conditions imposed by Israel.
“Usually anything under 38 millimetres is okay; anything above, it’s usually deemed as not acceptable,” Hughes explained.
“It is not a statement of dual use; it is just that this tent at this time is not allowed to enter Gaza … We don’t get the specifics,” said Karl Baker, head of the IOM’s Gaza programme.
Gaza’s Health Ministry reported on Saturday that 1,671 people had been killed since the “ceasefire” came into effect last October.
Meanwhile, 74,736 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.

items.title: Kenya targets paediatric HIV treatment gaps in World AIDS Day campaign
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21– Children, adolescents and young people account for 55 per cent of new HIV infections in Kenya, exposing a widening gap in the country’s fight against AIDS despite a significant decline in overall infections.
The latest figures show that Kenya recorded 13,936 new HIV infection
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21– Children, adolescents and young people account for 55 per cent of new HIV infections in Kenya, exposing a widening gap in the country’s fight against AIDS despite a significant decline in overall infections.
The latest figures show that Kenya recorded 13,936 new HIV infections in 2025, a 56.5 per cent reduction from 32,027 in 2021.
However, children aged 0 to 14 accounted for 3,396 of the infections, highlighting the challenges facing efforts to protect younger populations.
The figures have prompted health authorities to place children and young people at the centre of this year’s World AIDS Day commemorations under the theme, “Protect, Prevent, Empower: Ending AIDS Among Children, Adolescents and Young People.”
The National Syndemic Diseases Control Council (NSDCC), the National AIDS and STI Control Programme (NASCOP), county governments and civil society partners unveiled the programme on Friday, with activities set to begin with a national half marathon at Nyayo National Stadium on November 29 before spreading to all 47 counties on December 1.
The treatment gap among children remains particularly concerning, with Kenya’s HIV treatment cascade for those aged 0 to 14 standing at 79:60:52, compared with the national average of 93:91:87 across the three targets of diagnosis, treatment and viral suppression.
According to the Kenya HIV Estimates 2026, approximately 14,559 of the 69,330 children living with HIV have not been diagnosed, while another 21,908 have been diagnosed but are not receiving treatment.
Nearly half of children receiving treatment are also yet to achieve viral suppression, leaving them at risk of HIV-related complications.
Children account for 4.7 per cent of people living with HIV in the country but represent 11.5 per cent of AIDS-related deaths. Their fatality rate stands at 32.1 per 1,000, compared with 12.2 among adults.
The figures point to persistent challenges in preventing mother-to-child transmission and ensuring children diagnosed with HIV are promptly linked to treatment and retained in care.
Vertical transmission stood at 8.04 per cent in 2025, above the global elimination target of less than five per cent.
Douglas O. Bosire, Chief Executive Officer of NSDCC, said the government was shifting its attention towards the populations most affected by the remaining gaps in the HIV response.
“The 56 per cent fall in new infections since 2021 is a hard-won gain, but it will not hold if we lose our children. The Kenya AIDS Strategic Framework is being executed with children, adolescents and young people at the centre, and with the counties as co-owners of the response,” he said.
Bosire said county activities on December 1 would include public accountability forums where county leaders would be required to report on progress against targets for paediatric HIV diagnosis, treatment and care.
Dr Andrew Mulwa, Head of NASCOP, said the programme was prioritising the prevention of mother-to-child transmission, early infant diagnosis and improved retention of mothers living with HIV on treatment.
“We cannot accept a vertical transmission rate above 5 per cent, and we will not. We are scaling early infant diagnosis, strengthening retention for mothers on treatment and rolling out long-acting prevention, including the twice-yearly injectable PrEP now moving through 15 priority counties,” he said.
The programme will also strengthen sexually transmitted infection surveillance alongside HIV testing, particularly among young people.
The focus on children comes amid concerns over disruptions to HIV services and uncertainty surrounding external financing, which officials and civil society organisations say could undermine progress.
The National Empowerment Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Kenya (NEPHAK) raised concerns last year that some members were being charged between Sh500 and Sh2,000 for HIV tests that had previously been provided free of charge, pending clarification of coverage under the Social Health Authority.
Between April and June this year, some patients also received one-to-two-week supplies of antiretroviral drugs instead of the standard three-month refills.
Dr Samuel Kinyanjui, Country Director of AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) Kenya, said children living with HIV could lead healthy lives if they received timely diagnosis and uninterrupted treatment.
“A child born with HIV in Kenya today has every reason to live a full life. Whether she does is now a question of logistics and attention, not of science,” he said.
Alongside the national World AIDS Day programme, the Voices of Impact Awards Committee and AHF Kenya launched the second edition of the #VoicesOfImpact HIV and STIs Media Awards to encourage sustained reporting on HIV-related issues.
The awards, launched in 2025, recognise journalism, advocacy and digital storytelling that challenge stigma, promote dignity and support efforts to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
Entries opened on Friday, with the awards ceremony scheduled for June 18, 2027. The Kenya Editors’ Guild and Media Council of Kenya are supporting the initiative.
Victor Bwire, Director of Media Training and Development at the Media Council of Kenya, said responsible reporting was important in addressing stigma and ensuring the experiences of people living with HIV were represented with dignity.
“Accurate, stigma-free reporting is not a favour to the response. It is a professional obligation. The Council will support these awards because they reward the journalism our Code of Conduct already asks for: person-first language, informed consent, protection of children and adolescents, and verification against official sources,” he said.

items.text:
Pakistan drop Rizwan and Masood, but back Babar and Agha in overhaul
Former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood lose Pakistan central contracts, but Babar Azam and Salman Agha backed.
Pakistan’s Cricket Board has announced that it will drop former captains Mohammad Rizwan and Shan Masood in a major overhaul of its central contract list.
Saturday’s announcement, which expands the pool of contracted players to 38 from 30, comes a day after Pakistan won the second Test against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi, marking a first series win in two years.
“We are testing new players and these contracts are devised to let players focus on their specific format,” Pakistan selector Aaqib Javed told the media.
The board overhauled the Test squad after the second Test in its disastrous 3-0 defeat against England, sending seven players home and sacking head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed.
White-ball head coach Mike Hesson was given the Test team in a bid to lift the country, which is currently ninth and last in the 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle.
Besides Rizwan and Masood, white-ball specialist Saim Ayub, spinner Noman Ali and pace bowler Hasan Ali are among the 12 players who have been removed from contracts.
Test skipper Babar Azam and recently sacked Twenty20 International (T20I) skipper Salman Agha are in the top category of the 38-player list.
“The ‘AB’ category is for Test and ODIs, ‘A’ for Test-only, ‘BC’ for ODI and T20I players; ‘C’ for T20I specialists; ‘D’ for development players,” said Javed.
The new contracts run from July 2026 to June 2027. Players had been without central contracts since the expiry of the previous cycle in June.
The PCB had said at that time that only male cricketers who had played at least four tests, six one-day internationals or six Twenty20s in the previous 12 months would be eligible for central contracts.
Under the new system, contracts are split into five specialised categories: tests and ODIs, Test specialists, ODIs and T20Is, T20I specialists, and emerging players in the developmental pathway.
The new contracts run through June 30, 2027. Players had been without central contracts since the expiry of the previous cycle in June.

The Ministry of Roads and Transport said the move would allow moto
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – The Government is accelerating construction of the Rironi–Mau Summit Highway, with completed sections expected to be opened to motorists before Christmas to ease congestion along the busy Nairobi–Nakuru route.
The Ministry of Roads and Transport said the move would allow motorists travelling upcountry during the festive season to use sections of the expanded highway as contractors continue working on the remaining portions.
“The Government is fast-tracking works on the Rironi–Mau Summit Highway, with sections set to be opened to motorists ahead of the Christmas festivities to ease traffic congestion, enhance mobility and facilitate smoother journeys,” the Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.
The planned opening comes as thousands of Kenyans prepare to travel from Nairobi to the Rift Valley, Western Kenya and neighbouring regions for the December holidays, a period when the Nairobi–Nakuru highway traditionally experiences heavy traffic.
Roads and Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir has previously indicated that the Rironi–Naivasha section, measuring about 60 kilometres, would be accessible to motorists by Christmas 2026.
During an inspection of the works in November, Chirchir said sections that had received the initial layer of tarmac would be temporarily opened to traffic before contractors returned to apply the final asphalt layer.
“But before we do that, we’ll be opening this for traffic for a while in the coming weeks before we do the final layer,” he said.
The first layer of Dense Bituminous Macadam (DBM) has already been laid at Lari, marking a key milestone in the construction of the highway.
Chirchir said the Government had deployed additional equipment to accelerate the works, including 10 asphalt paving machines, with five operating from the Rironi side and another five from Naivasha.
He said the additional machinery would help contractors increase the pace of tarmacking, with the aim of covering about one kilometre daily on the targeted sections.
The project had initially been expected to meet an October 30 deadline for the Rironi–Naivasha stretch, but the timeline was pushed to December after construction delays.
Chirchir attributed some of the setbacks to difficulties in securing adequate supplies of bitumen, a key material used in road construction. He said geopolitical developments and supply chain disruptions had affected availability and slowed progress.
The Government has also urged motorists to exercise caution when using sections that remain under construction, follow instructions from traffic marshals and observe road safety regulations.
The Kenya National Highways Authority (KeNHA) has specifically advised drivers to ensure their vehicles are roadworthy and pay attention to signage and construction activity along the corridor.
The wider Rironi–Mau Summit project is expected to improve transport links between Nairobi, the Rift Valley and western Kenya, while supporting the movement of passengers and goods along the Northern Corridor.
President William Ruto officially launched the project at Manguo, near Rironi, in November 2025. Its implementation forms part of efforts to expand the major transport artery and address persistent congestion on the route.
Although the opening of completed sections is expected to provide some relief during the Christmas travel rush, construction will continue on unfinished sections and associated infrastructure, including works at the Naivasha Junction interchange

items.text:
Harry Kane: England and Bayern Munich striker vows to be back for ‘business end of season’ after ankle surgery
Harry Kane was withdrawn after 20 minutes of Bayern's Bundesliga game against Cologne; the injury comes days after the England captain became his country's most-capped player; Kane won the Ballon d'Or earlier this month; Michael Olise also taken off injured in 1-1 draw
Saturday 21 November 2026 11:26, UK
Harry Kane is targeting the "business end of the season" after undergoing surgery on a torn ligament in his left ankle.
Bayern Munich said the operation on the injury, sustained in Friday's 1-1 draw with Cologne, was a success but the 33-year-old is expected to be out for months as a result.
Kane wrote on social media: "The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it's an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027.
- How Bayern Munich fell in love with Harry Kane
- Kane becomes first Englishman to win Ballon d'Or for 25 years
- 'A cinderella story': Kane's journey from EFL loans to Ballon d'Or
"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season!
"Tough times don't last, tough people do" - my guy @edelman11 (Julian Edelman, three-time Super Bowl winner with the New England Patriots) told me this one!
"Thank you for all the messages! Alles gut."
Kane - who became England's most-capped player last week - sustained the injury when he was scythed down in the area by Cologne defender Joel Schmied, who reached Michael Olise's low cross first but clattered into the Ballon d'Or winner's left leg in his follow-through at the back post.
The England captain writhed in pain and, although he gingerly got back to his feet and initially soldiered on, it was clear he could not continue and he hobbled off the field alongside two physios after treatment.
Kane had a quick exchange with Vincent Kompany, who was back in the Bayern hot-seat for the first time in six matches after being diagnosed with meningeal irritation last month, before heading down the tunnel.
After the match Bayern confirmed Kane had torn the syndesmotic ligament and "will therefore be sidelined for the next few months".
Kane earlier this month signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029 - reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.
Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has bagged a scarcely believable 156 goals in 163 appearances in all competitions, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.
He went into the international break having a drawn a blank in his four previous matches for Bayern but he scored twice for England, including from the spot in their 3-2 Nations League win over Spain.
But after being forced off after 20 minutes at the Allianz Arena, replaced by Tom Bischof, Kane could now be facing a battle to be fully fit for England's two-legged quarter-final against Norway in March.
How many games will Kane miss?
A three-month period on the sidelines would rule Kane out for 11 Bundesliga games, the DFB-Pokal round of 16 tie against Hertha Berlin, as well as all four of Bayern's remaining Champions League league phase matches.
Providing his recovery goes to plan, that would give the striker just over a month to prepare for England's Nations League quarter-final.
The Three Lions face Norway in Oslo in the first leg on March 27, before the return leg at Wembley on March 30.
'This will concern Tuchel'
Henry Winter speaking on Back Pages Tonight:
"I've covered Harry Kane's career for so many years and there was a period where he had almost a chronic problem with his ankles.
"It's three months and, most immediately, it's Bayern Munich's concern. But England have the home and away Nations League quarter-finals against Norway in late March.
"The timeline would suggest he'll be back in that time, but thoughts with Thomas Tuchel tonight because he'll be absolutely concerned about this.
"He's such an important player. England's No 9. There's a bit of a gap behind him if you're looking for No 9s. I know Jude Bellingham can play there and that's probably the long-term plan. But this is hugely alarming."

items.title: Quality indigenous tree seed key to climate-resilient restoration in Eastern Africa
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – The success of landscape restoration efforts in Eastern Africa will increasingly depend on the quality and origin of tree seeds, as climate change alters rainfall patterns and threatens the survival of newly planted trees.
Experts have warned that planting trees without cons
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – The success of landscape restoration efforts in Eastern Africa will increasingly depend on the quality and origin of tree seeds, as climate change alters rainfall patterns and threatens the survival of newly planted trees.
Experts have warned that planting trees without considering their suitability to future climatic conditions risks undermining restoration investments, calling for greater investment in quality indigenous seeds and stronger community participation in tree seed production.
The issue featured prominently at the first Eastern Africa Indigenous Seed Conference, held from November 17–20 at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa in Nairobi, which brought together farmers, researchers, policymakers, seed custodians and development partners to strengthen farmer-managed seed systems across the region.
Sammy Carsan, Agroforestry Specialist at Landscape Alliance, said selecting appropriate seed sources was critical to ensuring trees planted today could survive changing environmental conditions in the years ahead.
“The tree you plant today has to survive the climate of future years. And that depends on the seed you choose today,” he said.
Carsan said restoration practitioners needed to consider tree species characteristics, local environmental conditions and projected climate changes when selecting seeds, warning that unsuitable choices could leave restored landscapes vulnerable as temperatures rise and rainfall becomes increasingly unpredictable.
Roeland Kindt, Senior Ecologist at Landscape Alliance, highlighted the role of scientific research and digital tools in helping practitioners identify suitable indigenous tree species and seed sources for different locations.
He showcased the organisation’s Global Useful Native Trees (GlobUNT) database, which provides information on useful tree species and supports evidence-based decisions on species selection and seed sourcing.
“The underlying principle is simple. We need to have the right tree in the right place, using the right seed source. And digital tools are helping us to do that,” he said.
The tools can help restoration practitioners assess the suitability of native species under different climatic conditions and identify appropriate seed sources for specific planting locations, an important consideration given the ecological diversity of Eastern Africa.
Beyond environmental restoration, experts and community initiatives highlighted the economic opportunities presented by indigenous tree seed production, particularly for farmers and rural communities.
Indigenous tree seed collection, production and nursery enterprises can provide income and employment opportunities while supplying planting materials for conservation and restoration programmes.
Paul Mwanza, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Palma Mukuyuni Tree Nursery, said indigenous trees offered communities an opportunity to develop viable businesses while contributing to environmental conservation.
“You can generate income and create a business with indigenous trees, so it is something we should embrace,” he said.
The discussions underscored the importance of involving farmers and local communities across the seed value chain, from collecting and conserving indigenous seeds to producing seedlings and supplying restoration initiatives.
Such participation could strengthen local seed supply systems, create alternative livelihoods and ensure communities benefit from growing investments in landscape restoration.
The conference also highlighted the need to connect scientific research with traditional knowledge and practical conservation efforts, with experts emphasising that successful restoration requires collaboration between researchers, farmers, policymakers and seed enterprises.

items.summary:
Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but the bar for triggering NATO’s collective defence clause remains high.
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on
items.text:
Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but the bar for triggering NATO’s collective defence clause remains high.
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
What happened in Poland?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Why did a Russian missile enter Polish airspace?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace, and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5, each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
Why has this happened now?
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
