items.title: Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
items.summary:
Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
- Published
Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.
A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead
items.text:
Jeers, injuries and doubters - White's journey back to the top
- Published
Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.
A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead in Madrid. They hung on - just - meaning White will always be remembered as the player who scored that winner.
But, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.
The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.
He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.
Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.
The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.
It hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.
But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal's key players.
- People don't know full story behind England exile - White 
  - Published9 November
- 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages 
  - Published5 days ago
White's England journey
"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never said anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.
The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.
After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.
His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.
That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.
White, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.
Tuchel was keen to back his player and said in the build-up to the Spain game that he hoped that the chapter was closed on White being booed by his own supporters.
"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White said of his return to England.
White said in that same interview that he would make the same decision again that he did at the World Cup, but it was now time to move on.
His displays show exactly where his mindset is for his country.
He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.
This new era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.
Chelsea defender Reece James is out with injury. He is a big favourite of Tuchel's but cannot be relied upon for every game due to injuries.
White is a key player for the Premier League champions, reliable in defence and a threat in attack while being physically imposing. There is a lot for Tuchel to like.
And with three of his Arsenal team-mates on the pitch as England won the game, and Bukayo Saka to return, White brings the positives of the cohesion of a club side to Tuchel's team.
Arsenal supporters not surprised by his performances
Arsenal supporters will not be surprised by White's excellent performances for England.
Since signing for the Gunners in 2021, not many players can say they have played more of a crucial role in Arsenal's rebirth under Mikel Arteta.
Such is the importance of White, the Gunners attack does not flow as freely when he is not in the side to link up with Martin Odegaard and Saka as he relentlessly produces overlapping runs - a trait he showed when he scored England's third in Madrid.
His team-mates regularly say he is one of the fiercest competitors in training, and he has regularly shown his mentality when it looks as though things are going against him with his club side.
Arsenal signing Timber and a number of injury issues looked to have had White nearing an exit but, such is his determination, each time a challenge comes up he manages to turn it around.
White is a unique character within football, and has even said he doesn't watch the game away from the training ground, but his passion for his profession cannot be doubted.
Gunners fans will know that the level of passion he displayed in Madrid is something he shows every time he is on the pitch for his club side.

items.title: Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?
items.summary:

items.text:
They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.
But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.
It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.
If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.
According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.
They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.
The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?
On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.
“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”
Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.
Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.
Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”
When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.
When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.
Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”
One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.
‘The numbers have to be right’

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear a

items.title: Van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Sykes in Grand Slam quarters
items.summary:
Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals
Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts
items.text:
Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals
Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22
Friday 20 November 2026 18:41, UK
Michael van Gerwen is through to his first premier ranking quarter-final in over a year but he is up against an opponent he probably did not expect.
Van Gerwen put in a stellar display in a battle of two darting juggernauts when he defeated James Wade 10-8 to make it through to the final eight at the Grand Slam of Darts.
The 'Green Machine' battled hard against everything Wade threw at him and, with a late surge and some superb finishing, he got the victory over the line.
Now, he is preparing for a quarter-final in Wolverhampton but instead of the predicted clash with world No 2 Luke Humphries, he is up against the 72nd-ranked player on the Tour in Tom Sykes.
Sykes pulled off a stunning final-leg victory over Humphries to make the quarter-finals on his debut at the major.
The Dutchman was impressed with what he saw from the 'Castleford Tiger' and knows that if he can beat Humphries, then he needs to expect the unexpected.
"Tom did really well against Luke. I didn't expect that, I think no one expected that, because this is the first time he's played such a long format on such a big TV appearance," he said.
"A win is a win and moving forward I think this gives me a lot of confidence.
"I have to face Tom who had a fantastic game against Luke, 100 average, loads of 180s, so I need to make sure I am prepared for anything.
"He is a fantastic player; he's been doing really well lately on the Tour, but now he has to deal with the fact that he's going to be first to 16. He's never been in this situation, so it will be new for him as well.
"But don't get me wrong, if you can beat Luke, he can beat anyone, so I need to make sure I prepare myself for the worst."
Van Gerwen has had well-documented ups and downs in his darting career over the last two years but has had glimpses of the levels everyone knows he can reach, his massive win against Wade the latest.
He admitted that the victory, and the manner of it, helped him overcome some demons about his own game and he is now looking to turn that into consistency.
"Yes, I did (overcome some demons). Of course, when you're not doing what you are capable of, it can be a really frustrating game," Van Gerwen added.
"But then to finally do it and also in the way how I did it, I think that gives me energy also towards the next game.
"I always believe in my own ability, otherwise I wouldn't be here. If I think I can't believe in myself anymore, that's the day I have to stop playing darts.
"But that day is not there, and it won't be there in the next few years, it is as simple as that.
"My consistency is starting to get better, my belief in my own ability starts to get better, if you also look towards the Pro Tours and everything, my game starts to get somewhere, and that's what you want, that's where you put the work in and the effort.
"That is how darts is, and darts can be a really cruel game, but at the moment I am still in so that's a good thing."

items.title: Antonelli fastest but Verstappen on pole after dramatic Las Vegas qualifying
items.summary:
Las Vegas GP: Kimi Antonelli fastest but Max Verstappen on pole from George Russell after dramatic qualifying
Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying but a five-place grid penalty for a new engine means Max Verstappen will be on pole from George Russell for the Las Vegas Grand Prix; watch Sunday's
items.text:
Las Vegas GP: Kimi Antonelli fastest but Max Verstappen on pole from George Russell after dramatic qualifying
Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying but a five-place grid penalty for a new engine means Max Verstappen will be on pole from George Russell for the Las Vegas Grand Prix; watch Sunday's race at 4am (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event
Saturday 21 November 2026 05:30, UK
Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a five-place grid penalty means Max Verstappen will start on pole position from George Russell.
New Formula 1 world champion Antonelli will start sixth due to a grid penalty for exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation and surprisingly went fastest in a hectic end to Q3.
The Mercedes driver only just crossed the line in time to start a final flying lap and was helped by a huge slipstream from the Racing Bulls throughout the lap to beat Verstappen by 0.258s.
- Las Vegas GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports

Russell was 0.331s behind Antonelli but the Verstappen-Russell front row cannot be missed when the lights go out at 4am UK time on Sunday (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event, after the pair made contact in final practice.
Neither driver was penalised as Verstappen was given a warning for driving erratically when trying to stop Russell from gaining track position in final practice earlier on Saturday.
McLaren's Lando Norris will start third with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar in fourth and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad will start in fifth, his highest career grid position.
Oscar Piastri qualified seventh but the McLaren driver has a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation, so will start 17th, so Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh instead.
Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto had great pace throughout qualifying but were caught up in the traffic chaos in Q3 on the out laps, so only qualified ninth and 10th.
Ferrari had a disaster as they struggled in the cold conditions and on the long straights, so both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were knocked out in Q2
It is the first time no Ferrari driver has reached Q3 since the 2024 Canadian Grand Prix and Hamilton was shocked both he and Leclerc did not get through.
Due to the grid penalty for Piastri, Leclerc will start 10th and Hamilton in 11th for Sunday's race.

items.title: Cummins to remain captain after 'unanimous support' from Cricket Australia
items.summary:
Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain, given 'unanimous support' by cricket board amid 'Sandpapergate' fallout
Pat Cummins confirms he will "100 per cent support" forum Cricket Australia has set up following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations; CA chair David Boon rejects notion Cummins' i
items.text:
Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain, given 'unanimous support' by cricket board amid 'Sandpapergate' fallout
Pat Cummins confirms he will "100 per cent support" forum Cricket Australia has set up following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations; CA chair David Boon rejects notion Cummins' integrity has been "compromised" amid varying accounts from players of 2018 ball-tampering scandal
Saturday 21 November 2026 05:28, UK
Pat Cummins will remain as Test and ODI captain after being given "unanimous support" by Cricket Australia, with the skipper confirming he will take part in the independent forum launched following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations.
Cummins' position had been under increasing scrutiny since Cameron Bancroft wrote a detail-filled account of the scandal in the West Australian newspaper, backing up Khawaja's claims that every member of the 2018 side was aware of the sandpaper plot.
Bancroft - the player caught on camera trying to alter the condition of the ball in South Africa eight years ago - said he was stirred to break his silence by Cummins' vehement denials of knowledge of the scheme in a press conference last week.
- Pat Cummins faces fresh scrutiny over Sandpapergate claims
- Sandpapergate: News and reaction to ball-tampering scandal
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
After Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met Cummins in Sydney on Friday, a statement released on Saturday read: "In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian Cricket and the welfare of all concerned.
"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."
Cummins prepared for 'difficult conversations' in forum
Cummins, who is set to lead Australia in a four-Test series at home to New Zealand from December 9, with the first match in Bancroft's native Perth, said: "Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility.
"I have and never will take that lightly.
"David (Boon) and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.
"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed.
"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."
Boon: Cummins' integrity has not been compromised
Boon added: "We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.
"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised.
"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn.
"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there.
"We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course."

items.text:
BJ Callaghan said he remains fully focused on leading Nashville SC through the Major League Soccer playoffs, amid links to replacing Mauricio Pochettino as United States men's national team head coach.
"For me, it's not about me. We've earned ourselves to get to the playoffs here and my job is to be a leader of this team and one of the leaders in this club," Callaghan told reporters on Friday.
- Pochettino: 'Massive' pressure with USMNT makes me better coach for Man United
- Ex-U.S. coach Arena: Federation doesn't 'have a clue' how to replace Poch
- MLS playoff Round 1 predictions: Who will move on to the conference semifinals?
"My focus is 100% on the players, the staff, the fans and overall this soccer club to make sure what happened in the regular season, we can make it an extension into the playoffs because we have more things to achieve here."
Pochettino departed his role as U.S. coach this week to become Manchester United's new coach. U.S. Soccer announced under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo will lead the team during the December international camp while the search for Pochettino's replacement is underway.
Callaghan previously served as an assistant to then-USMNT coach Gregg Berhalter before taking over interim charge in 2023. He led the group to the Concacaf Nations League title and reached the semifinals of the Gold Cup later that year before Berhalter was re-appointed.
Callaghan joined Nashville in 2024 and turned the team into a trophy-winning side.
Nashville lifted the U.S. Open Cup in 2025, when defeating Austin FC, and earned the 2026 MLS Supporters' Shield. Callaghan also inspired the Eastern Conference team to break the league's record for most points in a single season, with 77 points in 34 games, shattering Inter Miami's previous tally.
Nashville will now face FC Cincinnati in the best-of-three round one playoff series starting on Sunday.
Former Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City coach Pep Guardiola has been the biggest name linked to replacing Pochettino. Before his departure following a Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal win over Haiti on Tuesday, Pochettino encouraged anyone interested to take the job.
"It's the perfect moment to arrive to the [U.S. Soccer] Federation," Pochettino told reporters at a roundtable Monday. "Everything is in the right direction. I think, of course, take [it]. Take it because he's going to find really good people, good players. The player can fit for his style; the National Training Center that wasn't [there] before."

items.text:
ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
- Published
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.
In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.
At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?
If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

NINLIVE
The Nine Inch Nails live archive
Explore shows, download recordings, stream audio, and follow the tape trail across every era. Fan run, not affiliated with the band.
From the archive
The Future Is Here - ninlive Streaming 1988-2026
Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.
I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.
Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

items.text:
It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.
It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.
I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.
One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.
Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.
But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.
So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.
And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.
Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.
Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.
Past
Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.
John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.
In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.
To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.
Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.
Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,
“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”
S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.
McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.
The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.
The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:
(at me home)
(walkable home car)
(walkable home driveway)
(drivable car shop)

items.text:
The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
“… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859
[Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.]
I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven. I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code.
At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line (Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?
For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.
David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.
Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!
All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.
Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves. And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds. And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?
My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.
The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted?
It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation:
Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to…
Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak…
Dana: We should still fix the leak.

items.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
items.summary:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has b
items.text:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.
Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.
Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.
Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.
Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.
Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviating concerns about AI’s energy consumption.
Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.
“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani

A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eu
items.text:
Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

items.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167 year-old Riemann Hypothesis — and a human did, too
items.summary:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and des
items.text:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
The Hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.
Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …
The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.
For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.
But that comment was followed by twenty readers reacting 🤯.
It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source language that essentially helps verify mathematical proofs.
Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.
Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.
Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.
Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”
In a brief introduction his proof, which he said is the result of twelve years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While
items.text:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”
Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”
Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.
We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.
So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.summary: Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doin
items.text:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:
- First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
- If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
- If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.
What is the right code for this?
If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
- Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
- Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
Why AI won’t push back
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.
Your new job is to architect
AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
- Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
- Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.
Your future as developer
In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

items.title: Chips can survive the space environment. Can their financing?
items.summary:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data cente
items.text:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and re-sell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Research Index, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above the Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near-term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that buildout by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center buildout. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, how when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Company, Sophia Space, Orbital and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terrafab, in the US, but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

items.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary:
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:
- Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time bl
items.text:
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:
- Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions, which is formalized in Lean here.
- Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization. Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof.
- Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task.
See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

items.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has solved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. items.text:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has solved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics, and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary:

Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another
items.text:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (v1), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

items.text:
'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus
- Published
Already circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent days.
Not for the first time, Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus landed himself in hot water with the powers-that-be for criticising match officials.
After receiving a six-match ban for questioning the integrity of referee Andrea Piardi and television match official Matteo Liperini in South Africa's defeat by France last week, Erasmus has been defended and condemned.
There is no doubt, however, over where the Springbok camp stand, with assistant coach Mzwandile Stick throwing his support behind Erasmus.
"He's been hands-on with our team [in the build-up], and we're in a good space," Stick said on Friday.
"Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no-one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure."
Erasmus also said South Africa let their country down against France, with captain Siya Kolisi bristling at a suggestion that it was a "dramatic" assessment.
"It might sound dramatic to you, but to us it means so much more," Kolisi said during his pre-match news conference.
"Rugby has done a lot for our country, and it's done a lot for many of us who come from South Africa.
"We know how happy people are and what the mood is like when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it.
"When we play, we think about the people back home. We don't take representing the country lightly because we represent every single person in South Africa when we put on that jersey."
Ireland v South Africa
Nations Championship
Saturday 21 November, 16:40 GMT
Aviva Stadium, Dublin
Live on 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary
While Erasmus has dominated headlines this week, he will not be in attendance at Aviva Stadium on Saturday.
Instead, in a bizarre twist, the two-time World Cup winner will host a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel, with the conditions of his suspension prohibiting him from matchday contact with players and management.
Erasmus was not the only South African to receive a suspension this week with back row Jasper Wiese banned for four games for a dangerous ruck clearout against France.
While Wiese's fate did not attract the same level of scrutiny, South Africa's sense of injustice will perhaps be fuelled by the sight of Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast on Saturday.
As predicted by Erasmus, Prendergast was cleared to face the world champions after being cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fiji back row Peceli Yato.
"I will tell you now for free, if that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," said Stick.
"If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle."
Ireland focused on erasing scrum pain
Focused on erasing the pain of last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, Ireland have sidestepped questions about Erasmus this week, with head coach Andy Farrell opting not to comment on his opposite number's suspension.
Irish captain Dan Sheehan said the commotion has not "affected the squad at all".
"Obviously it's a big media story for fans to get behind, but in terms of us playing the match it has zero impact," he said.
While there may be added scrutiny on referee Christophe Ridley, Sheehan said he plans to leave the official alone unless compelled to bring something "major" to his attention.
The Irish skipper has enough on his plate anyway. In addition to leading his side against the back-to-back world champions, Sheehan has been thrust into the number eight role.
The 28-year-old has won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker but moves to the back row with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney all ruled out.
Ireland hope Sheehan's inclusion in the back row will facilitate his powerful ball-carrying capabilities, but he insists he is not going to "overthink" it.
"I just get on with stuff. Like, eight on my back, just pick the ball up and go," said Sheehan, whose only previous start in the position was in Leinster's win over Munster last month.
"It can't be that complicated. That's my approach to it, to be honest."
Had it not been for the furore surrounding Erasmus, chances are the pre-match talk would have been dominated by scrums.
Last year, Ireland were shown five cards and conceded six penalties and a penalty try during a chastening night against the Springbok scrum.
That set-piece shellacking may have given the Irish pack nightmares over the past 12 months, and while South Africa won nine scrum penalties against France, Kolisi expects a closer contest in Dublin this time.
"Their scrum is much better than it was a year ago," he said.
"You can see they're getting penalties. But our focus is not on what they're going to do. It's about making sure we stick to our plans and do what we need to do in the scrum."
The Springboks have been boosted by the return of record cap holder Eben Etzebeth, but his second-row partner Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury on Friday. He has been replaced by Franco Mostert, who was not originally in the matchday squad.
Ireland - who have lost their past six contests against New Zealand, France and South Africa, the three teams above them in the world rankings, by double-digit margins - have also been forced into a late change, with Thomas Clarkson replacing Sam Illo as the replacement tight-head prop.
The myriad permutations mean Ireland and South Africa could meet again in the finals weekend at Twickenham.
Either way, Saturday's sold-out contest in Dublin promises to deliver enough drama to tide fans over until next year's World Cup in Australia, where they could contest the final.

items.title: I'll never buy Framework hardware again
items.summary:
TL;DR:
